LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- The romantic comedy "New In Town" puts co-stars Renee Zellweger and Harry Connick Jr. at odds through most of the film. But behind the camera, the story was completely different, the pair told CNN. Harry Connick Jr. and Renee Zellweger enjoyed working with one another on the set of "New In Town." "I had a great time. [Connick is] such a nice guy. He shows up on set and makes everyone laugh, and it's just a nice day at work," Zellweger said. Connick agreed, saying the off-camera friendship with his co-star made the on-camera experience an enjoyable one. "Renee is the type of person that I got to know quickly. Well, I became friends with her quickly. She's a very mysterious, wonderful young lady," Connick said. Directed by Jonas Elmer, the film follows Zellweger as Lucy Hill, a Miami, Florida-based corporate shark who travels to a small Minnesota town to oversee the closing of a small factory. Upon arrival, Lucy clashes with the factory's union representative, Ted Mitchell, played by Connick. As the two begin to understand one another, their icy relationship soon melts into romance. But the romance between Lucy and Ted is only one side of the story. Zellweger said she was instantly drawn to the role for its humor. "I loved the physical comedy part of Lucy Hill's experience. I laughed out loud when I imagined the scenarios, and I could not wait to go and play around with that," she said, "I wanted to go to work every day and laugh, and I did." Famous for her roles in such comedies as "Nurse Betty" and "Bridget Jones's Diary," Zellweger is no stranger to the comedic scene. With "New In Town," the actress was eager to once again play a part that would make audiences laugh. "I think the laughter, that's therapeutic," she said. At a time when the country is struggling through a financial recession, Connick said, "New In Town" provides that necessary therapy. While the film centers on the troubles of one rural American town, it showcases a dilemma familiar to the entire country. "I think there's a good balance of what people are really feeling right now, and you walk away from this movie with a real feeling of hope and like, 'We're going to be all right,'" he said. "New In Town" opens in theaters everywhere this Friday. CNN's Jack Hannah contributed to this story.

# Renee Zellweger and Harry Connick Jr. warm up to romance in ‘New in Town’

**By CNN Entertainment**

Renee Zellweger and Harry Connick Jr. may play an unlikely couple in the romantic comedy “New in Town,” but the actors said the film’s frigid setting helped create a warm atmosphere among the cast.

Zellweger stars as Lucy Hill, an ambitious Miami executive sent to a small Minnesota community to reorganize a manufacturing plant. Focused on climbing the corporate ladder, Lucy initially clashes with the town’s close-knit residents — and with Connick’s character, Ted Mitchell, a union representative and devoted single father.

The story gave Zellweger a chance to explore both physical comedy and the familiar romantic-comedy tension between two characters who begin on opposite sides.

Connick said their contrasting roles made the relationship fun to develop. Lucy arrives convinced that she understands what the town and its factory need, while Ted is protective of the workers and skeptical of the outsider brought in to change their lives. As the pair get to know one another, their conflict gradually gives way to mutual respect and romance.

Much of the movie was filmed in Manitoba, Canada, where the cast worked in genuinely cold conditions. Zellweger and Connick have described the weather as an important part of the experience, giving the actors an immediate sense of the isolation and discomfort Lucy faces when she trades sunny Florida for an icy Midwestern winter.

The cold also became a source of camaraderie. With the cast bundled in heavy coats and working through wintry outdoor scenes, the off-camera environment echoed the film’s message about relying on the people around you.

For Connick, already known as a Grammy-winning musician as well as an actor, “New in Town” offered a relatively grounded romantic lead. Ted is less interested in impressing Lucy than in defending his neighbors, a quality that helps challenge her assumptions about success and community.

Zellweger, whose romantic-comedy credits include the “Bridget Jones” films, said the appeal of Lucy’s journey was not simply that she falls in love. The character also discovers that the people she initially dismisses have skills, loyalty and values that cannot be measured solely through corporate reports.

Directed by Jonas Elmer, “New in Town” also features Siobhan Fallon Hogan and J.K. Simmons. The film combines workplace comedy, small-town culture clashes and romance, with Lucy’s transformation unfolding against a landscape of snow, factory floors and community gatherings.

For Zellweger and Connick, the movie’s central idea was straightforward: Sometimes being sent far outside your comfort zone is exactly what it takes to find a new sense of home.

# **Cold Comfort: *New in Town* Finds Romance, Friendship and Recession-Era Hope**

Renée Zellweger arrives in *New in Town* dressed for a corporate takeover, not a Minnesota winter. As Lucy Hill, an ambitious Miami executive, she heads north in sleek clothes and high heels to reorganize a small food-processing plant. She expects an efficient business trip and a quick return to the sun. Instead, she encounters subzero temperatures, stubborn employees and a community whose survival depends on decisions made in distant boardrooms.

Lucy’s assignment is to reduce the plant’s workforce, but the job becomes more complicated as she gets to know the people behind the numbers. Among them is Ted Mitchell, played by Harry Connick Jr., a widowed father and labor representative who is immediately suspicious of the polished outsider. Their early encounters are combative, with Lucy defending corporate logic and Ted insisting that the factory is the town’s economic heart.

The friction gradually softens into romance. Lucy also forms ties with her talkative assistant, Blanche, and other residents whose warmth contrasts with the weather. When she learns that the company intends to close the plant altogether, Lucy must decide whether to protect her career or help the town fight back. A locally inspired product gives the workers a possible route to independence, turning the story into more than a fish-out-of-water comedy: Lucy’s transformation is complete when she begins treating the community as partners rather than liabilities.

That warmth was not confined to the screen. Zellweger and Connick developed an easy off-camera friendship during production, a connection reflected in their relaxed banter and willingness to tease each other in interviews. Connick spoke fondly of Zellweger as both a gifted colleague and a genuine friend, while Zellweger praised the musician-actor’s humor and grounded presence. Their rapport helped make Lucy and Ted’s courtship feel less like a conventional romantic-comedy mechanism and more like an ongoing contest between two people who enjoy challenging one another.

Zellweger also embraced the movie’s physical comedy. Lucy’s designer wardrobe, precarious footwear and refusal to admit that she is unprepared for the cold make her a natural target for snowbanks, ice and other wintry humiliations. Rather than keeping the character immaculate, Zellweger throws herself into the slips, tumbles and awkward scrambles. The comedy works because Lucy’s dignity matters so much to her: every pratfall punctures the controlled image she has built.

Released in early 2009, amid layoffs and deep recession anxiety, *New in Town* carried an unexpectedly timely premise. Connick emphasized that the film offered hope at a moment when many viewers were worried about losing their jobs and communities were confronting the disappearance of longtime employers. The movie does not pretend that economic upheaval is painless. Its optimism comes from people pooling their skills, adapting and refusing to accept that a corporate decision must be the final word.

That message gives the film’s familiar ingredients—small-town eccentrics, opposites-attract romance and snowbound slapstick—an added weight. Lucy comes to Minnesota intending to make a factory leaner. She leaves with a different understanding of success: one measured not only in profits or promotions, but in loyalty, ingenuity and the lives sustained by a workplace.

For Connick, that communal resilience was the movie’s central reassurance. For Zellweger, the journey offered ample room for both emotional change and exuberant physical comedy. Together, their friendship and chemistry helped turn *New in Town* into a warm-hearted story about discovering, in the coldest possible setting, that reinvention does not have to happen alone.
